To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

left ventricular pacing alone was no better than biventricular pacing for exercise tolerance, left ventricular function, or left ventricular remodeling in patients with heart failure, a left ventricular ejection fraction ≤35%, and a QRS complex ≥120 milliseconds.

in patients with heart failure and left bundle branch block, left ventricular (LV), but not biventricular pacing, was superior to right ventricular pacing in reducing left ventricular volumes and improving left ventricular ejection fraction.
LV pacing alone is not superior to biventricular pacing in patients with heart failure and a wide QRS complex.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the effects of pacing on the left ventricular (LV), right ventricular (RV) and biventricricular (BiV) function and remodeling in patients with left bundle branch block and heart failure.
the study of the effects of pacing the left ventricle (LV) compared to pacing the left and right ventricles simultaneously on the exercise capacity, LV ejection fraction and LV end-systole volume.
the development of novel methods for the treatment of patients with cardiac arrhythmias and heart failure.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
LV pacing is not inferior to BiV pacing, but that BiV pacing is superior to LV pacing in terms of exercise tolerance and reverse LV remodeling in patients who are not candidates for CRT.
biventricular pacing is the most effective pacing strategy in patients with heart failure and a wide QRS complex, but that LV-only pacing may be considered as a second-line option.
LV and BiV pacemaker therapies are not equivalent and that LV pacing should not replace BiV pacing as a first-line therapy in heart failure patients with LBBB.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
biventricular pacing is better than LV pacing, but that LV pacing is better than RV pacing.
LV pacing alone is not superior to biventricular pacing, but nonresponders to biventriculer pacing may respond favoribly to LV pacing.
LV pacing is not inferior to BiV pacing and there are a subset of BiV pacing nonresponders who may respond to LV pacing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
LV-only pacing is not better than biventricular pacing.
LV pacing is not inferior to BiV pacing in patients who have a wide QRS complex, but that it may be a useful option as a tiered therapy.
left ventricular (LV), or single-site, pacing is not superior or inferior to biventricular, or multisite, pacing for patients with heart failure and left bundle branch block.
